title: Compact disc
description: Digital optical disc data storage format
wiki_lead:
The compact disc (CD) is a digital optical disc data storage format co-developed by Philips and Sony to store and play digital audio recordings. It employs the Compact Disc Digital Audio (CD-DA) standard and is capable of holding uncompressed stereo audio. First released in Japan in October 1982, the CD was the second optical disc format to reach the market, following the larger LaserDisc (LD). In later years, the technology was adapted for computer data storage as CD-ROM and subsequently expanded into various writable and multimedia formats. By 2007, over 200 billion CDs (including audio CDs, CD-ROMs, and CD-Rs) had been sold worldwide.
Standard CDs have a diameter of 120 mm (4.7 in) and typically hold up to 74 minutes of audio or approximately 650 MiB (681,574,400 bytes) of data. This was later regularly extended to 80 minutes or 700 MiB (734,003,200 bytes) by reducing the spacing between data tracks, with some discs unofficially reaching up to 99 minutes or 870 MiB (912,261,120 bytes) which falls outside established specifications. Smaller variants, such as the Mini CD, range from 60 to 80 mm (2.4 to 3.1 in) in diameter and have been used for CD singles or distributing device drivers and software.
The CD gained widespread popularity in the late 1980s and early 1990s. By 1991, it had surpassed the phonograph record and the cassette tape in sales in the United States, becoming the dominant physical audio format. By 2000, CDs accounted for 92.3% of the U.S. music market share. The CD is widely regarded as the final dominant format of the album era, before the rise of MP3, digital downloads, and streaming platforms in the mid-2000s led to its decline.
Beyond audio playback, the compact disc was adapted for general-purpose data storage under the CD-ROM format, which initially offered more capacity than contemporary personal computer hard disk drives. Additional derived formats include write-once discs (CD-R), rewritable media (CD-RW), and multimedia applications such as Video CD (VCD), Super Video CD (SVCD), Photo CD, Picture CD, Compact Disc Interactive (CD-i), Enhanced Music CD, and Super Audio CD (SACD), the latter of which can include a standard CD-DA layer for backward compatibility.

History


Physical details

A CD is made from 1.2-millimetre (0.047 in) thick, polycarbonate plastic, and weighs 14–33 grams. From the center outward, components are: the center spindle hole (15 mm), the first-transition area (clamping ring), the clamping area (stacking ring), the second-transition area (mirror band), the program (data) area, and the rim. The inner program area occupies a radius from 25 to 58 mm.
A thin layer of aluminum or, more rarely, gold is applied to the surface, making it reflective. The metal is protected by a film of lacquer normally spin coated directly on the reflective layer. The label is printed on the lacquer layer, usually by screen printing or offset printing.

grok_lead: The Compact Disc (CD) is a digital optical disc storage medium consisting of a 12-centimeter-diameter polycarbonate substrate with a thin reflective aluminum layer, on which data is encoded as a spiral track of microscopic pits and lands readable by a low-powered laser beam to retrieve stored information such as audio, video, or computer data. Developed jointly by Philips and Sony starting in 1979, the CD format was finalized in 1980 through their collaborative "Red Book" standard, emphasizing high-fidelity digital audio playback with a capacity for up to 74 minutes of uninterrupted sound on a single side. The origins of the CD trace back to Philips ' early 1970s experiments with optical video discs, evolving into a dedicated audio project by 1974, while Sony pursued parallel advancements in digital recording techniques from its PCM audio systems. A pivotal alliance formed in 1979, driven by mutual goals to replace analog formats like vinyl records and cassettes with a durable, dust-resistant digital alternative; prototypes were demonstrated that year, leading to commercial launches in Japan and Europe in October 1982, followed by the United States in 1983. Initial CD players, such as Philips ' CD100 and Sony 's CDP-101, retailed for around $900â$1,000, but prices fell rapidly, enabling widespread adoption by the mid-1980s. Technically, CDs employ pulse-code modulation (PCM) for audio digitization at a 44.1 kHz sampling rate and 16-bit resolution, combined with cross-interleaved Reed-Solomon coding (CIRC) for error correction, which uses a multilayer scheme of Reed-Solomon codes with interleaving to detect and correct random errors as well as burst errors up to about 3,500 bits or defects up to 2.5 mm in length, and eight-to-fourteen modulation (EFM) to optimize data density on the disc's 1.2-millimeter-thick surface. The laser pickup tracks the spiral at a constant linear velocity of about 1.2â1.4 meters per second, converting reflected light variations into binary data that a player's digital-to-analog converter reconstructs into audible sound, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio exceeding 90 dB for near-perfect fidelity. Beyond audio CDs (CD-DA), the format expanded to include CD-ROM for data storage up to 650â700 MB, CD-R for recordable media using organic dye layers, and CD-RW for rewritable phase-change alloys, all maintaining backward compatibility with original players. The CD profoundly transformed the music industry, supplanting cassettes as the dominant format by the early 1990s and driving global record sales to a peak of approximately 2.4 billion units annually in 2000, thanks to its skip-proof playback, compact portability, and enhanced dynamic range that appealed to audiophiles and casual listeners alike. Its introduction spurred innovations in digital distribution and compression, laying groundwork for later technologies like MP3 files and streaming, though physical CD sales have since declined with the rise of online platforms. Despite this, the CD remains a key archival medium, with billions produced and ongoing use in professional audio and data backup applications.
